webTitle: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show

fields.headline: Trump approval ratings plummet to new low, polls show
fields.trailText: President says ‘I’m doing great’ despite polls showing 32% approval rating and loss of support from 2024 voters
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump’s approval ratings reached a record low on Monday, according to new opinion polls. A new Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Trump’s approval rating at a record-low 32%. That polling included the president losing support among independent voters and Latinos, who had backed him in 2024. The dip could prove dire for the Republican party a month before the midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. Before boarding a flight to Nebraska on Monday, Trump shrugged off questions about his approval ratings. “I’m doing great,” Trump told a reporter, who had asked about recent polls showing the president losing support among Latino voters, before blaming CNN and the media. But according to a NBC News/Telemundo poll release Sunday, 59% of Latino voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress, double the number that supported the party two years ago. According to that poll, just 24% of Hispanic Americans approve of Trump’s performance. Trump has spent the past few days campaigning across the country for Republican candidates, despite even conservative states starting to show the loss of support. Some Republicans have also started to distance themselves from the president over issues such as immigration as they attempt to hold on to local support. With Americans souring on the economy, the war with Iran, and other key issues they attribute to the administration, the impact of the negative sentiments could reach far and wide.

webTitle: Obama to appear at Abdul El-Sayed rally in critical Michigan Senate race

fields.headline: Obama to appear at Abdul El-Sayed rally in critical Michigan Senate race
fields.trailText: Former president to visit 10 days before election day as victory for progressive challenger could tip Senate balance
fields.bodyText: Barack Obama will head to Detroit this month to rally with Abdul El-Sayed, a show of establishment support for a progressive insurgent in Michigan, one of the most consequential Senate races in the country. The former US president will appear with El-Sayed and the gubernatorial nominee, Jocelyn Benson, on 24 October, the state’s Democratic party announced on Monday. The rally falls on the first day of the state’s in-person early voting period and 10 days before election day. “Get. Ready,” El-Sayed wrote on social media as he confirmed the appearance. The event is a significant endorsement for a candidate who survived tens of millions in an out-of-state ad blitz to beat the congresswoman Haley Stevens by less than a percentage point in August, making the contest a national proxy battle over the party’s direction. El-Sayed, a doctor and former Wayne county health director, ran on Medicare for All and a refusal to take corporate Pac money, and was backed by Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. He made opposition to US military aid to Israel and criticism of its conduct in Gaza central to his campaign, and has described Israel’s actions there as genocide. Aipac and its allies as a result spent a record-breaking $30m trying to stop him, and in total Stevens and her allies outspent El-Sayed’s side nearly nine to one on advertising, according to AdImpact. Stevens, a moderate, was backed by the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, incumbent senator Gary Peters, and the party establishment. Obama’s presence matters most in Detroit, where Black residents make up more than three-quarters of the population and where he is still highly popular. Stevens won Wayne county, which includes the city, with about 51% of the Democratic primary vote to El-Sayed’s 45%. Some ads backing her used old footage of Obama praising her, which critics called misleading because he had not endorsed in the race. Kamala Harris, the first Black and south Asian vice-president, campaigned with El-Sayed last month, and Obama phoned him after the primary. El-Sayed is running for the seat being vacated by the retiring Democrat Peters, against the Republican former congressman Mike Rogers, and the contest is one of a handful that will determine Senate control next year. Rogers was the Republican nominee in 2024, and lost that race against Elissa Slotkin, despite Donald Trump winning the state. A Marist poll of registered voters from late September had El-Sayed ahead 51% to 44%. Still, El-Sayed, who has sworn off corporate donations and made his opposition to big money in politics a theme of his campaign, traveled to New York for a fundraiser where top “all-star” donors were asked to give $57,800, split among his campaign, the Michigan Democratic party and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, with Ocasio-Cortez and the city’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, expected to attend, the New York Times reported. Obama has kept a relatively low profile this cycle, but is preparing a broader push. He has recorded about two dozen advertisements for Democratic candidates for governor and Senate, to be released in the coming weeks, and further stops are to be announced. Earlier this year he campaigned in Texas with the Senate nominee James Talarico and the gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, and featured in an ad for Josh Turek, the Iowa Senate candidate. This week he will headline a Washington fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, his first with the group this cycle.

webTitle: Republicans criticize Steve Hilton for ‘creepy’ innuendo-filled campaign ad

fields.headline: Republicans criticize Steve Hilton for ‘creepy’ innuendo-filled campaign ad
fields.trailText: Hilton faces heavy backlash from within his own party for ‘Just Try It’ ad amid his longshot bid for California governor
fields.bodyText: Steve Hilton, the Republican candidate for California governor, is receiving heavy criticism from members of his own party over a controversial, sexual innuendo-filled campaign ad that has been described as “creepy”. The video entitled “Just Try It, California” was released last week and depicts two young women with brightly colored hair, sitting on a bed in front of a pride flag in low lighting. One nervously says “I can’t believe I’m doing this”, while another strokes her hair and coaxes “don’t be nervous, it’s not that bad” before guiding her to fill out a ballot for Hilton and aggressively commanding “lick it”. The controversy comes as Hilton, a British former political adviser to David Cameron and Fox News host, is fighting to advance his longshot bid against Xavier Becerra, the former health secretary. With just a few weeks to go before the November midterm elections, Hilton is trailing in the polls. Sonja Shaw, the Republican nominee for California superintendent of public instruction, called the new campaign ad “creepy, weird, disturbing garbage”. “This is a clear example of exactly why good people are walking away from the Republican party. As a mother and someone who has fought to protect the innocence of children, this crosses a line. We have lost our way,” she wrote on social media. Michael Gates, the party’s nominee for state attorney general, also condemned the advertisement, stating that he “emphatically [denounced] the use of young women as a political tool”. Hilton faces tough odds in the deep blue state, where voters haven’t elected a Republican to lead since 2004. Polls have consistently shown Becerra with a significant lead over Hilton. Hilton is trying to rally California’s Republicans while converting Democrats and independents frustrated with the ever-increasing cost of living in California. In a video posted shortly after the ad was launched, Hilton said it had largely been positively received but that he recognized that people were offended, and that was not his campaign’s intention. “We were trying to make a point in a provocative way, in satirical way,” he said. “It grieves me that you’ve been upset by this. But I also want to ask you to understand what we are doing, why we’re doing it and to ask for some grace as well as understanding as we fight this campaign.” Becerra was quick to jump on the controversy, posting an article about his own support for Medicare for All with a line directed at his rival: “Steve, just try it!”

webTitle: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base

fields.headline: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
fields.trailText: A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran
fields.bodyText: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran. The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before. Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”. Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening. US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US. A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year. But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan. Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said. UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”. Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking. RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target. The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November. It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmac during fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base. Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute. Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged. No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later. Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

webTitle: Republican Ken Paxton admits forces in DC control his Texas Senate campaign

fields.headline: Republican Ken Paxton admits forces in DC control his Texas Senate campaign
fields.trailText: ‘I don’t control message or what we’re doing,’ scandal- hit state attorney general reportedly says at private event
fields.bodyText: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general chosen by Donald Trump to run as the Republican candidate for a Senate seat, admitted in private that his campaign was being controlled by outside forces in Washington DC. Paxton, who is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico, told people at a fundraising event in September that he had never felt such little control over his campaign because of outside influence. “I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from D.C.,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico. “I don’t control message or what we’re doing,” Paxton said. An unnamed attender told Politico that Paxton never explicitly said he was referring to Trump’s team controlling his campaign messaging but that Paxton’s comments arose during a conversation about the national political environment. Paxton’s campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement, “Campaigns don’t coordinate with Super Pacs, and that’s obviously what AG Paxton was referring to. “AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority which is why he’s on the ground every day talking to Texas, raising money, and taking his message directly to the people including with his statewide television buy that started over this past weekend,” Maddux said. Earlier this year, Trump chose Paxton to run against Talarico, a political newcomer who Democrats hope will flip Texas’s longtime red senate seat to blue in the midterm elections next month. Though Paxton has been a well-known conservative figure in Texas for years, he has also been embroiled in a series of scandals. Paxton was impeached in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust – though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife, Angela Paxton, also divorced him on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery. Polls show Paxton and Talarico neck-and-neck, with Talarico having a small lead over the Texas attorney general. A Fox News survey found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 49% among likely voters. A New York Times/Siena College poll found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 45% among likely Texas voters. A Marist University poll indicated Talarico had 50% while Paxton had 44% among registered voters. Paxton’s latest comments are the second reported critical remarks the Texas attorney general has made about outside involvement in his campaign. Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican National Convention for the midterms “dropped” his polling numbers. Asked whether the convention had negative consequences, Paxton replied: “So to be honest with you, the numbers – when we did that convention – it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.” Maddux told the New York Times that Paxton’s reported comment was “manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist”.

webTitle: Relatives of Epstein victim appear in attack ad targeting Republican congressman

fields.headline: Relatives of Epstein victim appear in attack ad targeting Republican congressman
fields.trailText: Family of Virginia Giuffre criticizes Colorado’s Jeff Crank for voting to block a vote to release the Epstein files
fields.bodyText: Two relatives of Virginia Giuffre, one of the most prominent Jeffrey Epstein victims who died last year, appeared in a political attack ad targeting the Colorado Republican congressman Jeff Crank, accusing him of refusing to meet with them. Sky Roberts, Giuffre’s brother, and his wife, Amanda Roberts, expressed disappointment that Crank had voted to block a vote to release the federal investigative files relating to Epstein. The couple claimed that Crank, who later supported the Epstein Files Transparency Act which authorized the release of a tranche of documents in a near-unanimous vote, refused to meet with them in Washington. “My sister Virginia was one of Jeffrey Epstein’s victims. She spent her life trying to expose the truth. After she died, we promised to carry on her fight,” Sky Roberts said in the ad backing Crank’s opponent, Democrat Jessica Killin. “But our own congressman Jeff Crank refused to meet with us,” Amanda Roberts continued. “Then, when he had the chance to expose the truth and release the Epstein files, he repeatedly voted to cover them up.” The couple have become increasingly politically active. Over the summer they urged senators on the Senate judiciary committee to block the confirmation of Todd Blanche as attorney general. They also criticized a decision by the Department of Justice to restrict the release of unredacted files to Epstein investigators in New Mexico. They also appeared at Donald Trump’s State of the Union address in February as guests of the Maryland congressman Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House judiciary committee. Epstein has become a major issue for Donald Trump amid public unhappiness over the presidential administration’s handling of the issue. While Democrats are largely focusing on economic issues ahead of the midterm elections, the Epstein issue has cropped up in some races, though the Colorado ad is the first to feature family members of an Epstein victim. An ad funded by a Democratic group in Maine accused the Republican senator Susan Collins of voting “with Trump to cover up the Epstein files” and “protecting child predators” and another political ad in Iowa accused the Republican congresswoman Ashley Hinson of accepting donations from people named in the files. They have not been accused of wrongdoing. “I would like to tell Ashley Hinson that I don’t trust you. If you can’t stand up for girls and women in Iowa and the rest of this country, why should I ever vote for you?” a woman says in the voiceover of the ad. The New York Times has identified 35 congressional races with ads that mention Epstein, though most appear to reference the financier in the context of the “Epstein class”, a phrase used to assemble opposition to an idea of unaccountable or excessive wealth in the US. The outlet noted that attack ads deploying “Epstein” lack reference to the reversals of the lawmakers positions on the document release. Sky and Amanda Roberts told the New York Times that they met with Crank’s district director after joining protests against his re-election in the district. “At the end of the day, the bare minimum of this job in this role is to hear your constituents,” Sky Roberts said, relaying his conversation with Crank’s aide. “How can you stay with your constituents and vote according to their needs if you have no idea what their needs are?” Simon Andriesz, a whistleblower and former Wall Street banker who alerted Congress to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick’s ties to Epstein, died by suicide last week.

webTitle: Trump’s former press secretary Karoline Leavitt to join Fox News

fields.headline: Trump’s former press secretary Karoline Leavitt to join Fox News
fields.trailText: Youngest press secretary in White House history left earlier this year after the birth of her second child
fields.bodyText: Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining her former boss’s favorite network, Fox News, as an on-air contributor, the channel announced on Monday. Considering that two of her predecessors from Donald Trump’s first administration, Sarah Huckabee Sanders and Kayleigh McEnany, had also joined Fox after leaving office, Leavitt was seen as a logical fit for Fox, on which she will begin providing commentary on 1 November. In the announcement, the Fox News chief executive, Suzanne Scott, praised Leavitt’s “authentic and sharp insight” and said her “first-hand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today’s political landscape”. In her own statement, Leavitt said she was “grateful for the opportunity”, adding, “I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms.” Leavitt, 29, who was the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year. She said at the time that she planned to spend more time with her family and take a role with the Trump-aligned Super Pac Maga Inc. When she announced her pregnancy in December, she became the first sitting White House press secretary to do so. During her tenure, Leavitt sought to reshape the White House media landscape. She moved to exert greater control over the press pool, the small group of journalists who closely track the president’s daily activities; created a “new media” briefing room seat, often filled by conservative commentators and pro-Trump personalities; and frequently clashed with reporters. One of Trump’s most steadfast defenders, Leavitt emerged as a key ally for the president and regularly drew praise from him during her time in the West Wing. Despite his long-term relationship with the network, which helped launch his political career, Trump still regularly criticizes Fox News for being insufficiently loyal, including a lengthy Truth Social post on Sunday criticizing the network’s morning show Fox & Friends for not airing his recent rallies. “Our people want to see our Rallies, and reports on our Rallies, on FoxNews, or they will very quickly stop watching (like I am doing right now!). Fox spends more time talking to Communists, Socialists, and Dumocrats, often without rebuttal, and MAGA is not, to put it mildly, happy.” He also repeated his familiar attacks on the left-leaning Fox News commentator Jessica Tarlov and criticized the network for cutting ties with longtime host Maria Bartiromo. But many of Trump’s former associates – and even his daughter-in-law Lara – remain Fox News regulars. Larry Kudlow, who served as his director of the national economic council during his first administration, was recently tapped by Fox to replace Bartiromo on Fox News’ Sunday morning lineup through the midterm elections next month.

webTitle: The surprising, cut-throat race for Los Angeles mayor

fields.headline: The surprising, cut-throat race for Los Angeles mayor
fields.trailText: Karen Bass is fighting for her political life as progressives battle to lead the US’s second-largest city
fields.bodyText: Karen Bass has never lost an election. But this fall, she faces the fight of her political life. Bass has roughly a month to convince voters that she should be elected to a second term as the mayor of Los Angeles. Given Angelenos’ broad dissatisfaction with the direction of the city, approval ratings on par with Donald Trump’s and a wave of anti-establishment sentiment sweeping American politics, she has a formidable challenge in city council member Nithya Raman. Chances are it’s not where Bass, who came back to run Los Angeles after a long and successful political career in Sacramento and Washington, had imagined she’d be. First there was Raman’s surprise entry into the race – hours before the filing deadline – then Bass’s decisive victory in the primary, when she eliminated the candidacy of TV personality Spencer Pratt. But with mere weeks to go, several polls have Bass trailing, some narrowly and some with wider margins. Los Angeles is a deeply blue city and the mayor’s race has become a bitter battle between two progressives who have come to represent the clashing wings of the Democratic party. Raman has the endorsement of the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, and is a longtime member of the chapter. Its large network of volunteers are knocking on doors across the city in the lead-up to the election, seeking to appeal to a multiracial coalition of working-class Angelenos and renters. Bass too is seeking to shore up her base. On a sunny Sunday afternoon in late September, she was in the middle of a marathon day of campaigning across Los Angeles with stops at six churches, a volunteer appreciation event and four more gatherings scheduled for the evening. “I’ll be going until about nine,” she said, seated at a picnic table in Ernest E Debs regional park on the city’s east side, after spending an hour greeting supporters. Her days are packed with campaign events and mayoral duties, she said, including leading the city’s transportation authority. “I have no idea what being bored is.” It’s a busy election season for both candidates. They both spoke at forums hosted by the Muslim Public Affairs Council and the Jewish Federation Los Angeles in September. The pair are tied in fundraising, with each campaign raising about $2.5m. Nithya Raman’s campaign did not respond to a request for an interview. ••• In early 2026, Bass appeared to be catching a break. For a year, she had faced persistent criticism over the city’s preparation and response to the Palisades fire in January 2025, as well as the fact that she was traveling abroad when the disaster began. Her popularity had begun to rebound after the Trump administration’s crackdown on anti-ICE protests in the summer of that year, and mass immigration raids across the region. Bass had spoken out forcefully against the operations, praising the role immigrants from around the world play in Los Angeles, and at one point personally confronted border patrol agents who had deployed to a park in an immigrant neighborhood. Her response appeared to be shaped by her years of experience organizing and deep ties to immigrant groups, and was appreciated by many in the city. By February of this year, several competitors, including the billionaire Rick Caruso, who faced off against Bass during her first run, had announced that they would not challenge her, easing the mayor’s path to victory. It also presented an opening. Nithya Raman, a progressive urban planner, had been on the Los Angeles city council since 2020. The DSA member shocked the political establishment that year when she beat out an incumbent Democrat backed by Nancy Pelosi and Hillary Clinton. Bass supported Raman’s bid for re-election to the council in 2024, and in 2026 the city councillor backed Bass’s re-election, calling her the most progressive mayor the city had ever seen. Hours before the filing deadline, however, Raman opted to run against Bass, surprising both allies and opponents. She told a reporter she felt the “call from Los Angeles … for change across the entire city”. Raman’s bid was initially a long shot, many political analysts agreed. Key portions of the city’s liberal base and large unions had already aligned with Bass. As the primary race unfolded over spring, it was Spencer Pratt who grabbed headlines. The former reality TV star and registered Republican decided to run for office after losing his home in the Palisades, arguing Los Angeles leaders were mismanaging the city, failed to do enough to prepare for the fire and were falling short in helping residents recover. He offered raw criticism of Bass, and his ads frequently went viral. Pratt’s performance in a debate appeared to boost his campaign as he sparred with the mayor while Raman struggled to find her footing and had comparatively little airtime. Donald Trump endorsed Pratt, a development political commentators said would hurt his candidacy in the deeply Democratic city. Bass emerged as the frontrunner in the contest and, initially, as Pratt appeared on track to upend the race, Raman seemed almost prepared to lose. Nearly a week after polls closed, it became clear she had narrowly eked out a win, beating Pratt by about 3.5%. The months that followed were largely quiet, noted Zev Yaroslavsky, the director of the Los Angeles initiative at the Luskin School of Public Affairs at the University of California, Los Angeles. “We had a whole summer where there was, at least to the average person, no campaign out there. Only this last week did advertising start to appear on television,” Yaroslavsky said in late September. ••• Now with ballots already on their way to voters, the final days of the election are fast approaching and Bass and Raman are eager to highlight their different approaches to voters. Their divide could be seen during a recent forum hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, in which Bass said she didn’t believe the term genocide was appropriate to describe Israel’s actions during the war in Gaza. Raman, who said she used the term after looking to experts, faced questions about an interview earlier this year with the streamer Hasan Piker and her relationship with DSA. In response, Raman called herself an “independent voice”, pointing to her disagreements and collaboration with DSA, and describing it as a big tent organization Raman picked up endorsements from the nearly 6,000-member DSA LA in September, as well as the Unite Here union. Rae Huang, another DSA member, had run in the primary, and the organization opted in the spring not to support any candidate. The decision to back Raman came after significant debate – she has been a DSA member for years but the organization censured her in 2024 for pursuing an endorsement from a Democrats for Israel group. Yet, the chapter praised Raman for working “tirelessly to lower housing costs and build more housing”, championing tenant protections and reforming how the city responds to homelessness, pointing to the drop in unsheltered homelessness in her district. The endorsement was a major win. Polling has indicated the majority of Democrats in the city view DSA positively and the organization has a large number of committed and experienced field workers, said Fernando Guerra, a professor at Loyola Marymount University and director of the school’s Center for the Study of Los Angeles. The operation was on display during a crowded postcarding event at Los Angeles Ale Works in late September and a canvassing operation in the westside community of Sawtelle. There is excitement around Raman, DSA members Patrick Padilla and Keshav Kundassery said, with unprecedented numbers of people showing up to field training. During canvassing, they said, they have found that the organization’s platform has broad appeal – including among many people who don’t identify as democratic socialists. “We’re coming to find that the status quo has not been serving everyday working Americans. And when I’m on the doors, I’m talking to people. People are just focused on how they can get by day to day,” Padilla said. In Sawtelle on a recent Saturday, Padilla and a group of five others gathered to prepare for door-knocking in the area. Organizers walked two first-time volunteers through training, advising them to “knock friendly” and that the activity was about “talking to your neighbors”. “If they’re a no, don’t push,” one facilitator said. This forms a core pillar of DSA’s operation and will be crucial for their candidates in the coming weeks. DSA has made major gains in Los Angeles and across the US, most notably with the victory of Zohran Mamdani in New York. The wave of wins is not just about DSA, Guerra argued, it’s about the anti-incumbent sentiment that has surged in recent years. “It’s the political establishment that people are voting against. And of course, [Bass] represents that,” Guerra said. ••• Earlier this year, a survey published by the UCLA Luskin School of Public Affairs found that Los Angeles county residents’ satisfaction with their quality of life had reached the lowest levels in more than a decade. Although it is not the hellscape that Donald Trump and high-profile Republicans portray it to be, the region faces real challenges common to major cities across the country, including rising costs and housing affordability. The city is one of the most expensive in the US for renters and homebuyers alike. While there has been a 17.5% reduction in people living on the streets under Bass, homelessness remains an entrenched problem, with nearly 44,000 unhoused people. Residents are frustrated about the region’s handling of the crisis. The Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority, a joint agency of the city and county, has been under increased scrutiny in recent months, both locally and by the Trump administration. The county announced this year that it would seek a financial review of the agency over its delayed payments to service providers. An audit released earlier this year found issues with the agency’s bookkeeping and accounting. The federal government suspended funding to LAHSA in June. Meanwhile, federal officials recently arrested two LA homelessness non-profit workers for allegedly misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars. Recent years have been particularly difficult, with the Trump administration’s deportation campaign hitting the region hard and Hollywood struggling. The city is also grappling with a huge budget shortfall. Raman has argued she is the candidate who can “meet this moment with honesty and urgency” while lowering rents, improving city streets, reducing homelessness and keeping Angelenos safe. “We can fight for a bigger, more joyful future for Los Angeles,” Raman has said. Bass is in a difficult position with low approval ratings, Yaroslavsky said, and serving as mayor is often thankless. “The mayor gets no credit for the things that go well, gets all the blame for the things that go wrong,” he said But the race isn’t over yet. Bass needs to articulate her vision for the city to win over voters and distinguish herself from Raman, said Yaroslavsky, who served on the LA city council and county board of supervisors for decades. To win, she’ll have to appeal to the unusually large share of undecided voters as well as those who supported Pratt, many of whom feel deeply disappointed in their options. “Honestly, I don’t feel like there is a viable choice for a Spencer Pratt voter,” said Nina Madok, who lost her home in the Palisades fire and has worked on recovery efforts. Madok noted that Bass’s staff had been supportive and present for Palisades victims, but said neither candidate appealed to her. It would take commonsense support and a recognition of the issues the city faces to get her backing, she said, adding that it would be a “hold your nose” vote. “I would never say never. But something drastic would have to happen,” she said. Of course, Madok added, “we know that in LA anything could happen – an earthquake, a flood, an El Niño around the corner, another fire. We’d have to see.” *** Bass is hopeful that her decades-long record in the city will propel her campaign forward. She got her start as a physician assistant at LA county general hospital and founded Community Coalition, a non-profit that built collaborative relationships between the Black and Latino communities to tackle substance abuse and violence prevention. Bass served in the statehouse and Congress and was under consideration to be Joe Biden’s vice-presidential candidate. At Debs park in September, a line of elected officials and community advocates rallied for the mayor as part of a Latinos con Bass volunteer appreciation event, while she stood among them wearing a Dodgers jersey and blue-and-white Nikes. “I’ve known her [since] she was an organizer. And she’s always been an organizer. So she’s just organizing in a different place,” said Angelica Salas, the executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (Chirla). “Fighting for LA is not something that is new to her.” A few hundred people gathered around park tables and food booths to hear Bass and her supporters speak, as families barbecued nearby. The speakers highlighted Bass’s record and criticized Raman, suggesting her decision to run was opportunistic. Bass still has deep pockets of support throughout the city. “She’s trying to make things better for the people, the city. She’s for the community,” said Joe Alcala, who attended the event with his granddaughter. “I’m so busy right now, I don’t even know who her opponent is.” People typically tune in to elections late, Bass noted as she sat down with the Guardian after the event, but they are beginning to pay attention. Asked about the wave of wins for progressive candidates, Bass said that she understood that people were demoralized and angry. She described herself as a lifelong progressive “fighting for change and not just blindly following the system”. “[I have] 45 days of making sure that I am visiting all of the places I’ve worked in a good part of my life, reminding people of what we have done and reminding people of what we’re going to do in the future,” she said. “Because an election is about the future, it’s not about the past.”

webTitle: Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered | Sidney Blumenthal

fields.headline: Vance wants voters to ‘give us another chance’. But he is cornered
fields.trailText: The vice-president’s recent remarks seek to maintain a posture of strength while they inadvertently expose political realities
fields.bodyText: JD Vance has parachuted into the midterm election campaign on a rescue mission in a new guise: a risk management consultant. Speaking in the flat language of the expert hired to identify threats, weaknesses and losses affecting a business’s reputation, he has presented his executive summary for limiting vulnerabilities and a scenario for averting disaster. “There’s a lot of good that’s been done, but there’s a lot of work left to do,” he informed his clients on 15 September about the words to use. “Give us another chance, or give us another couple of years, to continue to work on the amazing things that we’ve been doing for the past two years.” He turned the focus to harm reduction rather than total agreement and then shifted the equation to a negative binary choice. “Even if you don’t agree with us on every issue, the other party is consumed by craziness.” His proposal for a “another chance”, however, did not acknowledge harm, express remorse or offer any pledge to change. Skipping the apology avoided admitting error, wrongdoing or enlightenment. The lack of an apology allowed Vance – and Donald Trump – to maintain a posture of unwavering strength, to demand continued fealty and to maintain their pretenses. Vance’s strategy does double duty by firmly establishing his stake to become the prospective successor to Trump as the Republican presidential candidate in 2028. He himself embodies “another chance”. But his implicit self-characterization creates an indelible political identity that the man of many identities must carry forward through this campaign and the next. Every vice-president seeking to become president is inevitably “another chance”. Vance carries the burden of one of the most unpopular presidents of modern times. His gameplan depends upon more than calculated forgetfulness. Abject failure should be seen as “amazing” success. Explaining away Trump means never having to say you’re sorry. Vance’s plea for “another chance”, however, has not produced the desired effect. Instead of Maga minions aroused to march in a phalanx through Trump’s Arch of Triumph, Vance’s defensive positioning has dampened fervor while opening the door to criticism within his party. Beleaguered Republican Senate candidates who had been in lockstep with Trump have suddenly started to flake off. Yet even as they edge away, they still take timid steps. Mike Rogers in Michigan had previously argued that congressional efforts to limit Trump’s authority in the Iran war would “not be good for America” and dismissed concerns about rising fuel costs. “We’re going to be fine, we got plenty of oil,” he said. Senator Ashley Hinson in Iowa insisted that the US needed to “finish the job”, voting numerous times against invoking the War Powers Resolution to force an end to US involvement or curb executive authority without congressional approval. Then Rogers reversed himself, “I think the best option now is to wind it down … The time is now.” Hinson followed suit, pleading that “the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.” The panicked Republicans are not really defectors. None of them has offered a single reason why any Trump policy has been flawed, damaging or counterproductive. But now they want out, somehow to reduce their vulnerabilities. They demand an export ban on diesel as a panacea, which the Financial Times reports “wouldn’t be workable” and would have unintended consequences that would lead eventually to fuel price spikes. The Republicans without a cause are seeking “another chance” without being able to articulate a difference from the past. They are pivoting into a void. Having supported Trump down the line they would prefer not to be held responsible for the consequences. But their fracturing underscores that the president and the policies they supported are the source of their quandary. The Republican freak-out validates voters’ anxieties that continuing the Trump status quo carries unacceptable risk. Rogers, Hinson and others cannot be dismissed as Democratic complainers. Their attempt to distance themselves grounds the Democratic criticism in more than partisanship and undermines the simple choice of rejecting the Democrats as the radicals. Intra-party disintegration makes the Trump administration, not the opposition, appear more unpredictable and untrustworthy. The uneasy Republicans’ bid for “another chance” subverts Vance’s framing of the midterms as a judgment about who flew over the cuckoo’s nest. “So, to the American people, I’d say, send these people packing, put them in the mental hospital, do not put them in Congress, because even if you don’t agree with us on every policy issue, at least we’re motivated by common sense and American interest.” Vance’s pitch relies on vapid “common sense”, but when Republicans turn tail the illusion of irresistible power is shattered and the dogma loses its magnetism. It is the Republicans above all who are neutralizing Vance’s damage control. His request for “another chance” to manage voter dissatisfaction through relative comparison places a marker against which the uncertainty, doubt and fear of Republicans is gauged. At a pep talk to House Republicans, Vance suggested what he thought was a clever pointer about how to demonize Democrats. “And if you are one of the few Republicans who’s running against a Democrat who’s not that crazy, then just talk about Abdul El-Sayed,” he said. But Vance’s advice overstretched his less-than-crazy defense, not least with El-Sayed polling ahead of Rogers. Vance disclosed the hollowness and falsity of his strategy by acknowledging that Democrats are “not that crazy” and that the insinuation must be contrived, a trick he has done before. Vance’s insistence on making the election into a contest of who is crazier is his most self-defeating idea. In that competition, Trump will always be the winner. The Economist/YouGov poll, taken at the same moment Vance delivered his advice, showed that 51% of registered voters selected the word “dangerous” to describe Trump, alongside 53% choosing “corrupt” and 47% “out-of-touch”. Only 18% called him “steady”. Vance’s simplification discards the cult of personality in which the leader can do no wrong and ideology brooks no debate. The leader must always be uniquely capable, his words unassailable and the movement always winning, so much you’ll get tired of it. Vance’s imploring introduces an element of skepticism. He shifts the basis for support from zealotry to a cold calculation. Ideology is unmasked, vision lost, the leader becomes fallible. Without unquestioning belief, the cult of personality no longer is attributed magic but depends on risk management. When Vance confesses that it is the Trump administration that is the incumbent regime that must be defended and Republicans are banging to get out of Trump’s Iran war, resentment cannot be easily mobilized against “the deep state”, “the establishment” or “globalist elites”. When Trump rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese communist leader, Xi Jinping, he rolled it over the trope against Democrats as “communists”. Once again, “another chance” Vance has inverted his personal identity, contradicting the character he projected in Hillbilly Elegy, his foundation myth. Scourged by his dysfunctional upbringing he rejected the endless excuses of his alcoholic and drug-addicted mother and accepted the raw honesty and moral clarity of his “Mamaw” and “Papaw”, and found the road to redemption. Vance wrote urgently about the danger of false messiahs blaming scapegoats such as immigrants instead of offering hard truths of responsibility to working-class people. He depicted himself as a “cultural emigrant”, bearing authentic Appalachian values among the “elite” toward whom he had an “almost primal scorn”. In 2016, Vance referred to Trump as “reprehensible”, “an idiot”, and wondered to a friend if he was “America’s Hitler”. Vance wrote in the Atlantic that Trump was like “cultural heroin” and offered private advice to Hillary Clinton’s campaign, according to Chris Whipple’s profile of him in Vanity Fair. Vance was recruited to Silicon Valley as a venture capitalist set up by Peter Thiel of the Paypal mafia and co-founder of Palantir, who had notoriously stated: “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” When Vance ran for the US Senate from Ohio in 2022, Thiel bankrolled his campaign to the tune of $15m. Vance transformed himself into the stalwart Trump supporter. “I regret being wrong about the guy,” he said. But he didn’t explain the inner process of his Damascene conversion. After barely serving in the Senate, his new best friends, Tucker Carlson and Donald Trump Jr, promoted him to Trump into the vice-presidency. During the 2024 campaign, Vance cemented his latest new identity by scapegoating Haitian immigrants for supposedly eating pets. He confessed he made it up. “If I have to create stories so that the American media actually pays attention to the suffering of the American people, then that’s what I’m going to do,” he admitted. Vance announced he had converted from evangelical Protestantism to Catholicism, and he has clashed with Pope Leo. “I think it’s very, very important for the pope to be careful when he talks about matters of theology,” Vance said in April about Leo, channeling Trump’s spirit of retribution. Leo replied that he had “no fear” of the Trump administration for “speaking out loudly of the message of the Gospel, which is what I believe I am here to do”. In June, Vance published another memoir, Communion: Finding My Way Back to Faith, in which he credits Thiel – “possibly the smartest person I ever met” – for his conversion, but mentions Leo only in passing, avoiding reference to his feud. Vance identifies himself with a narrow “postliberal” rightwing movement. The Catholic theological historians James M Patterson and Thomas D Howes, in their new book, Why Postliberalism Failed, explicitly describe Vance’s newfound faith as “an ideology that failed”. Vance’s ritualistic non-apology, “another chance”, is a sheer power play that repudiates his original transformation as described in Hillbilly Elegy in which he achieves mature reflection by the grace of accepting personal responsibility. More dangerously to him, his opportunism may have closed off his opportunity. Vance has cornered himself into perhaps not simply his latest but his last political identity – the unapologetic apologist – from which he cannot escape through the election of 2028. In calling for “another chance”, Vance may have run himself out of identities. Sidney Blumenthal, former senior adviser to President Bill Clinton and Hillary Clinton, has published three books of a projected five-volume political life of Abraham Lincoln: A Self-Made Man, Wrestling With His Angel and All the Powers of Earth. He is a Guardian US columnist and co-host of the Court of History podcast

webTitle: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual | Steven Greenhouse

fields.headline: Trump’s recent statements on the economy are even more bonkers than usual
fields.trailText: Our ‘genius’ president is revealing his ignorance of economics, fueling concerns about the threat he poses to the world
fields.bodyText: Donald Trump recently made a bold claim about his abilities, writing on Truth Social: “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” But in the days before and after that post, Trump made one mind-boggling statement after another, including one that raised the possibility of cutting off all trade with dozens of the US’s trading partners. The president’s statements had many experts questioning not just his intelligence, but also whether he – and the outlandish policies he was proposing – were a clear and present danger to both the US economy and the world economy. Public respect for Trump’s economic sense has fallen so low that just 7% of Americans think he should take the lead in regulating AI, according to a recent WSJ poll. Responding to Trump’s reckless statements, one prominent advocacy group, Republicans Against Trump, derided him as “Dumbest. President. Ever.” Economists and corporate executives were especially alarmed by two Trump statements. First, he wrote on Truth Social: “I’ll stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Federal Reserve doesn’t cut interest rates. The second disconcerting statement was: “If we stopped Trading with every country that we have a Deficit with, which is most of them, we would make, at least, 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year.” Not only is Trump’s arithmetic childishly silly here, but any college student who took Econ 101 knows that if a trade-dependent nation like the US suddenly ended all trade with dozens of countries, that would lead to economic disaster. What’s more, it was worrisome that Trump views himself as almighty emperor with the power to singlehandedly halt hundreds of billions of dollars in trade. If Trump ordered the US to terminate all trade with every place with which it has a trade deficit – that includes China, Mexico, Taiwan and the European Union – many US manufacturers would quickly find themselves in desperate straits, unable to obtain critically needed computer chips, rare earths, auto parts, aluminum and much more. As a result, many factories would be forced to close. Not only that, many farmers would be crippled because they couldn’t import the fertilizer they need, while many homebuilders would have to stop work because they couldn’t import needed lumber. Those were by no means Trump’s only recent mind-boggling statements. Two days before the Federal Reserve raised its short-term interest rates to 3.75% to 4% to combat inflation, Trump was on a tear, badgering and bullying the Fed, telling it not only not to raise interest rates, but to cut rates sharply. “We should be at 1% or half a percent,” Trump said. Again, anyone who took Econ 101 knows that cutting rates so sharply and so low will push prices skyward at a time when the Fed and consumers already think inflation is too high. And let’s not forget that Trump was the guy who promised to reduce prices on day one as president. With that statement, the self-described “stable genius” president showed his utter failure to understand one of the most basic teachings of Econ 101 – when interest rates are extremely low, like 1%, that heats up the economy and that revved-up economic activity fuels inflation. The University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers called Trump’s demand for a 1% interest rate “the dumbest thing ever said by a president”. Then there was this whopper. Trump said that if the Fed bowed to his demands and slashed interest rates, “we could have a GDP [growth] of 14, 15, 16 and 20.” Those numbers are absurd, fantastical. Considering that the US economy grew at a moderate 2.2% rate in this year’s second quarter and rarely grows faster than 5%, talk of 20% growth is delusional. Since the second world war, the US economy has grown at a rate at 20% or higher just once. That happened in the third quarter of 2020 due to extraordinary circumstances – in that quarter, myriad businesses rushed to reopen after the worst pandemic in a century caused many to suddenly shut down during the previous quarter. (GDP plunged at a 28% rate that quarter.) Then there was this colossally wrong-headed statement about trade: “The word ‘Deficit’ is nothing more than a fancy word for LOSS.” Trump coupled that assertion with his misbegotten statement that the US would magically be $1.5tn richer if it terminated all trade with every nation with which it has a deficit. This shows an infantile understanding of trade – and a stunning blindness to its mutual benefits. To explain how inane Trump is being here, let’s hypothesize for a second that in the US-France trade relationship, the only goods traded are wine and bourbon. Under Trump’s ludicrous logic, if the US buys $2bn of wine from France, and the French import $1bn worth of Kentucky bourbon, the resulting $1bn trade deficit means the US is simply giving away $1bn to France. Trump bafflingly sees that as an outright $1bn loss. Blinded by ignorance, ideology or an idée fixe, Trump fails to see that that’s not a harmful $1bn “loss” – rather, Americans are getting $1bn worth of fine wine to enjoy. No doubt wine lovers across the US see that as a gain and certainly not as a $1bn loss. Bottom line, Trump’s delusional statements on the economy show that he is becoming more detached from reality and from rational understanding of how the world works. One can’t help but wonder why his economic advisers don’t stop him from making such ridiculous and at times dangerous statements. If Trump turns his absurd economic notions into reality, as he has done in his ugly, unnecessary trade war with Canada, that will be more bad news for Americans. Voters should realize that Trump, with his failure to grasp basic economics, is a danger to the economy. He has brought us higher prices, slower GDP growth, and constant economic chaos and uncertainty. His tariffs and disastrous war against Iran have hit the great majority of Americans in their wallets and pocketbooks. Tragically, Trump’s Republican supporters in Congress either cheer him on or remain dismayingly silent while Trump does serious damage to the economy and to the finances of millions of struggling families. Americans shouldn’t forget this when they vote in November’s midterm elections. Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issues

webTitle: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?

fields.headline: Monday briefing: You asked, we answered – how will the US midterms go?
fields.trailText: In today’s newsletter: As Americans get ready to vote on whether the Republican party remains in control of Congress, our Washington editor talks about the disconnect between Trump and his supporters
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Later today, Donald Trump will be in the state of Nebraska to rev up supporters as he kicks off a campaign blitz of rallies ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November. If his early speeches are anything to go by, cornhuskers can anticipate poll denial, accusations of veganism and an expletive ratio that my nine-year-old would love. And Nebraskans may love it, too: aside from one “blue dot” district in Omaha, Republicans argue their support is steady in the state that has easily backed Trump three times. This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote, and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base. I asked First Edition readers what you really want to know about the US midterms. Today, in a happy exercise in newsletter cross-pollination, I put your questions to our Washington editor Ankita Rao, who runs our US elections newsletter The Stakes. First, the headlines. Weekend roundup UK politics | The Greens in England and Wales have formally adopted a policy that equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state. Schools | Lawyers and campaigners have condemned the “horrifying” scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools after a Guardian investigation revealed thousands of sexual offences against under-13s are reported to police each year. Brazil | Brazil’s presidential race will go to a second round after the far-right candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, beat the incumbent leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, but failed to secure the outright majority he needed to avoid a runoff. Environment | A study of Europe’s summer paints a grim picture for the future, with doctors and climate scientists calling on governments to stop burning fossil fuels, shade buildings, green cities, and install air conditioning in hospitals, schools and care homes. US military | The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base. In depth: ‘We are prepared for anything’ You’d be forgiven, readers, if the state of US politics is perplexing you. On the one hand, there are voters who have little faith in the president’s war in the Middle East and are increasingly angry about his inability to make daily life more affordable at home. On the other, Trump has promised a “big surprise” come 3 November – and polls have predicted the wrong results for previous elections. As Ankita Rao set out in The Stakes in September, her team of reporters across the US are hearing the same things in almost every community they’ve spent time in: • Americans feel their lives are dictated by an elite class that goes beyond political parties – best summed up by Democratic senator Jon Ossoff’s use of the term “Epstein class”. • People are exhausted by an ongoing crisis in affordability of childcare, healthcare, food and gas. • Many have lost trust in institutions, from hospitals to schools. With this deep knowledge of the mood of the country, she is the woman to answer your questions. Over to you. *** Who still believes in Donald Trump? Johanne, Quebec, Canada Ankita’s short answer is that it might be the other way around: a lot of Americans don’t feel they’ve been presented with a better option yet. This was evident during primary season, when both Democrats and Republicans went for candidates “who they felt would actually stick it to the man”, says Ankita, rather than regurgitating established party platforms. After all, that was what so many hoped to get with Trump – but those voters who had flocked to him as the anti-establishment leader, or the man who represented something beyond the two-party system, now see him aligning himself with big tech and other corporate interests, particularly this last term in office. There’s a serious disconnect between Trump and his supporters, Ankita tells me. His previously impressive political instincts have faltered “partly because he can’t see beyond his own fixations” – be that his ballroom, the war in Iran, or the unfettered growth of AI. As one Ohio voter told us at the weekend: “I’m sorry, but I don’t give a shit whose name is on the Kennedy Center.” *** Has Trump got a decisive ‘dirty trick’ up his sleeve? Bron Purkiss, England A big concern for First Edition readers is election interference: how Trump has already restricted voting and what dirty tricks he might still try. Will he try to ignore the election results – and how would the Guardian report that? Ankita joined Guardian US seven years ago as voting rights editor, launching our multiyear democracy project. “We had four reporters on that, but now they’re part of the larger politics team, and election integrity has become essential to our coverage,” she says. In the months leading up to the midterms, Trump signed executive orders seeking to assert more control over voting methods, and in a Time magazine interview last week, he refused to rule out declaring a national emergency around elections to implement them. “So we are prepared for anything,” says Ankita. Legal challenges in individual races are “almost inevitable”, she says. “We know the states where the election systems are fully controlled by Republicans, and we’re ready to move everybody there if we see anything strange happening”. Fear of election rigging is high in the communities Guardian reporters are visiting. “We hear this a lot from Democrats who are worried about making sure their vote counts, and more nervous about using mail-in ballots.” This September edition of The Stakes covers Trump’s attempts to restrict postal voting – which is how almost one-third of Americans vote. Ankita suggests this could result in higher turnout. Early data in the deeply red state of Florida, for example, showed voter registration among Democrats already very high. “There’s a sense that ‘we need to go out in droves and make sure that all of these wins are very decisive, so that nobody can question them’.” *** Would Republican losses limit Trump’s excesses? Peter Alexander, England Ankita tells me she doesn’t make predictions any more – a lot can change in a few short weeks – but if an election was called tomorrow “it looks as if the Democrats will absolutely win the House and most likely win the Senate”. The mechanics of voting mean that it will take a decisive majority in both chambers to act as a genuine bulwark against Trump, says Ankita, before adding the weighty caveat that Trump sidestepped congressional authorisation altogether ahead of the Iran war. Nonetheless, she anticipates a slew of investigations after the midterms, launched in the House and then requiring the Senate to move them forward. For example, there are already calls for an investigation into revelations that a Russian oligarch bankrolled part of Donald Trump Jr’s recent wedding in the Bahamas. *** How will democratic socialists influence policy decisions after the midterms? Feride Hekimgil, Turkey This is a “huge question”, Ankita agrees, as progressive candidates capture the enthusiasm of voters desperate for radical change. While the number of Democratic Socialists actually elected is likely to only be a handful, it could become a “very vocal group”. What’s not clear yet is how they will act once in the Congress. Ankita points to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, one of the country’s most prominent democratic socialists: “She was very clear about her affiliation when she ran, but she hasn’t been that type of lawmaker where she exists to stop the party from doing certain things. She has been much more strategic and collaborative with establishment Democrats.” It remains to be seen whether an augmented group after 3 November takes a similar route or choses a more hardline stance, in particular on Israel’s decimation of Gaza, which has already created gaping divisions in the Democratic party. *** One more thing In an early edition of The Stakes, Ankita described her morning bike ride to the Guardian’s Washington office, navigating National Guard trucks and reflecting on the militarisation of her city since the last election. I wanted to ask her, as a citizen as well as a journalist, how that influences the way she approaches this election. It can’t be overstated, she tells me, how it changes your day-to-day life: “It adds a layer of subtle fear. I’m not actively scared about walking around DC, but it feels as if things could escalate really quickly.” Will it hold people back from voting, or at least displaying their preferences? Quite the opposite, she tells me. “Places where we see this military presence – in Minneapolis, or LA, or DC – are such vocal, largely Democratic cities that people are undeterred.” “There are double the number of lawn signs,” she says. “It’s defiant.” • For more from Ankita and the Guardian US politics in the run-up to the midterms, sign up to The Stakes 2026 here The week to come Tuesday | ABC News is suing the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) over its licence review, and on Thursday its hearing will take place. The broadcaster claims the review, ordered by Donald Trump in April over comedian Jimmy Kimmel’s comments about the US president, is a “retaliatory campaign” in violation of its first amendment rights. Wednesday | Kemi Badenoch is to speak at the Conservative party conference in Birmingham. This day also marks the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks by Hamas. In London, the Met are asking organisers of a pro-Palestinian student march to move the event. Thursday | Holborn and St Pancras will hold its byelection. The seat belongs to former prime minister and Labour party leader Keir Starmer, who held it from 2015 until his resignation in September. What else we’ve been enjoying Helena Horton’s sweeping interview with the Royal Horticultural Society boss Clare Matterson is an absorbing conversation about everything from her high hopes for Andy Burnham, the roles of gardens in public health and the RHS’s £2.3m roadworks compensation. “Who is gardening for in the 21st century?” Matterson asks. “Is it for a small elite band of people, or is it for everybody?” Craille Maguire Gillies, newsletters team If you didn’t catch it yesterday, our interview with the actor John Boyega, recounting the impact of seeing his close friend Damilola Taylor die when he was a child, is deeply moving. Poppy Noor, newsletters team Who doesn’t love images of funny animals? This photo gallery of laughing bears, a sexy mantis and a truly angry bird is worth a look and chuckle. Craille Sport Football | Manchester City came from behind on two occasions to beat Arsenal 4-2 ⁠in the Women’s Super League on Sunday, keeping the champions top of the table. Racing | Formula One drivers have issued a damning condemnation of the sport’s engine regulations that caused the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to open with scenes of cars stopping on track and unable to accelerate because of software problems. Max Verstappen got his first win of the season at the chaotic race. Football | The Republic of Ireland’s manager Heimir Hallgrímsson has called on Uefa to keep his side away from Israel in future draws after a pair of fixtures he admitted “has been tough on us all”. The front pages The Guardian leads with “Horryfying scale of child-on-child sexual abuse in schools revealed”. The Times splashes with “Badenoch to pledge a bonfire of green laws” and the Mail has “Kemi’s common sense blueprint”. The Mirror, on Badenoch’s pledges to cut benefits, goes with “Bad to the future”. The Telegraph has “Andrew takes police to court over arrest” and The Financial Times says “Hopes for record year in dealmaking punctured by interest rate increases”. The i Paper runs with “Man City owners’ link to Burnham’s No 10 North site after ‘sweetheart deal’ with UAE firm”. And the Sun leads with a story on the romance between Mark Chapman and Kelly Cates, headlined “Love match of the day”. Today in Focus Colonialism for clicks? The influencers targeting uncontacted tribes Features writer Elle Hunt and Indigenous activist María José Andrade Cerda on the growing phenomenon of influencers around the world trying to reach uncontacted tribes. Cartoon of the day | Tom Gauld The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Five years ago, Barbara Scully sat in her car crying. Trying to find work after taking time to raise her children, she found herself facing closed doors. “I presume it was the fact that I was 50 and had a 10-year gap where my career used to live [while she was raising children],” she says. “I sat in the car on the driveway in tears, thinking: that’s it, I’m washed up, I’m done.” Then something changed. “Once I pulled myself together, I thought: OK, if this were one of my kids, what would I tell them? … Look at what it is you enjoy doing and try to make that work for you.” Scully relaunched her career for the sixth time, as a broadcaster and comedian, and feels happier than ever. “I am on a mission to try to tell women in particular not to fear getting older; to embrace it, to push back against all the bullshit about how you should be fighting ageing,” she says. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.
